title: Maximum Frequency of an Element After Performing Operations II
statement:
Exactly `numOperations` operations are applied to the integer array `nums`. Each one chooses an index that no earlier operation chose and adds to that element an integer of your choice between `-k` and `k` inclusive (`0` is allowed, so an operation may leave its element unchanged).

Once every operation is done, count how many elements hold each value. Return the highest count you can arrange for a single value.
signature: int maxFrequency(int[] nums, int k, int numOperations)
notes:
## Intuition

Fix the final value `x`. Elements already equal to `x` count for free. Any other element within `k` of `x` can become `x` with one operation, and elements further away never can. So `x` reaches `same + min(numOperations, reachable - same)`, where `reachable` counts the elements in `[x - k, x + k]`. The only question is which `x` to try:

- If `x` appears in `nums`, its copies are free, so try every distinct value.
- If it does not, the frequency is `min(numOperations, reachable)`, and the best `reachable` is the largest group of values spanning at most `2k`: they all meet at the lowest one plus `k`.

After sorting, both counts are pointer scans. The brute force instead counts each candidate (`v - k`, `v`, `v + k`) over the whole array in O(n²).

## Approach

1. Sort `nums`.
2. For each run `[start, end)` of equal values `target`, advance `low` past values below `target - k` and `high` past values up to `target + k`. Then `same = end - start`, `reachable = high - low`, and `best` takes `same + min(numOperations, reachable - same)`.
3. Slide a window `[left, right]` that keeps `nums[right] - nums[left] <= 2k`. All `right - left + 1` values can meet at `nums[left] + k`, so `best` takes `min(numOperations, right - left + 1)`.
4. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 4, 5]`, `k = 1`, `numOperations = 2`. Target 1: `[0, 2]` holds only itself, frequency 1. Target 4: `[3, 5]` holds 4 and 5, so `1 + min(2, 1) = 2`. Target 5: `[4, 6]` holds 4 and 5, again 2. The widest window spanning at most 2 is `[4, 5]`, worth `min(2, 2) = 2`. The answer is 2.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; each pointer then moves at most `n` times.
- Space: O(1) beyond the sort.

## Pitfalls

- The best value may be missing from `nums` entirely: `[1, 3]` with `k = 1` and two operations both become 2.
- Copies of the target cost no operation; only the other reachable elements are capped by `numOperations`.
- Two elements `2k` apart can still meet (at their midpoint), so the window width is `2k`, not `k`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `best` | highest frequency found so far |
| `start`, `end` | the run `[start, end)` of copies of `target` |
| `target` | candidate final value taken from `nums` |
| `low`, `high` | indices `[low, high)` hold the values within `k` of `target` |
| `same`, `reachable` | copies of `target`, and all elements within `k` of it |
| `left`, `right` | window of values spanning at most `2k` |
